payload.instructions: Preserve all candidate IDs and distinctions. Broader parent themes organize evidence; they do not imply measurement equivalence.

themes.disagreements: contradictions, weak signals, and proxy distinctions
evidence_ids: at most 12 representative supplied modeling evidence IDs
themes.interpretation: common or complementary evidence
themes.name: theme

themes.disagreements: Varying strength of treatment prediction across candidates, with disease_status (102) showing a weaker signal than ecog_performance_status (109).
themes.interpretation: General disease and performance status markers that strongly correlate with both treatment assignment and outcome prognosis.
themes.name: Functional and Disease Status

themes.disagreements: Dyspnea (106) and dyspnea_on_exertion (107) primarily show confounding signals, whereas dyspnea_severity (108) exhibits strong evidence for both confounding and effect modification.
themes.interpretation: Respiratory symptoms showing consistent prognostic importance and treatment prediction, with graded severity providing heterogeneity signals.
themes.name: Respiratory Burden

themes.disagreements: Different primary drivers of modification: recurrence (101) is supported by R-learners and causal forests, while dizziness (103) is supported by univariable effects and causal forests.
themes.interpretation: Clinical markers that primarily signal treatment-heterogeneity without strong main-effect confounding.
themes.name: Neurological and Recurrence Markers

themes.disagreements: dural_sinus_patency (104) shows moderate predictive forest support for both roles, while edema (110) and dysplasia (105) remain largely unsupportive.
themes.interpretation: Anatomical and pathology findings with weak or inconsistent evidence for causal roles.
themes.name: Anatomical and Pathology Findings

themes.disagreements: Nausea (feature 119) shows significantly weaker signals compared to the functional domains, though it retains some predictive forest support.
themes.interpretation: Candidates measuring physical, cognitive, emotional, and global health status exhibit strong and consistent signals for both treatment prediction and outcome prognosis across univariable and forest-based models.
themes.name: EORTC QLQ-C30 Quality of Life Domains

themes.disagreements: Employment status is a dominant confounder, whereas emphysema specifically shows a strong signal for effect modification via Causal Forest.
themes.interpretation: Baseline characteristics showing a mix of strong confounding (employment status) and combined confounding with treatment-heterogeneity (emphysema).
themes.name: Baseline Health and Demographic Status

themes.disagreements: EGFR mutation status has moderate support for treatment heterogeneity, but lacks the strong treatment-prediction signal seen in other confounders.
themes.interpretation: Biomarkers with varying degrees of influence; EGFR mutation status shows a credible signal for effect modification and prognosis, whereas enzyme elevation is largely uninformative.
themes.name: Molecular and Biochemical Markers

themes.disagreements: While feature 126 is a very strong treatment predictor, its lack of outcome signal suggests it may be an instrument rather than a confounder.
themes.interpretation: Candidates exhibiting high support across univariable and forest models for both treatment assignment and outcome prognosis, suggesting potential confounding roles.
themes.name: Strong Treatment and Outcome Predictors

themes.disagreements: Feature 124 also shows moderate signals in main treatment and outcome models, which may overlap with its effect modification signal.
themes.interpretation: Candidates where the most credible signals appear in effect-estimation models (R-learners, Causal Forests) rather than main effect models.
themes.name: Treatment-Heterogeneity Signals

themes.disagreements: Feature 123 shows a penalized main treatment signal, but lacks the complementary outcome or effect signals required for a more active role.
themes.interpretation: Candidates with low overall support or signals primarily limited to outcome prognosis without strong treatment prediction or effect modification.
themes.name: Weak or Prognostic-Only Signals

themes.disagreements: Variation in the strength of treatment prediction; while all exhibit some predictive forest support, only feature_133 shows meaningful support in penalized main models.
themes.interpretation: Family history measurements consistently emerge as candidates for effect modification, with an additional confounding signal for myocardial infarction history.
themes.name: Family History

themes.disagreements: Feature_139 exhibits only weak, inconsistent signals across all roles, contrasting with the strong effect-modification signals of fatigue and neutropenia.
themes.interpretation: Clinical symptoms and toxicity markers primarily demonstrate evidence for effect modification and outcome prognosis.
themes.name: Clinical Status and Toxicity

themes.disagreements: FGFR1 amplification shows a distinct and stronger treatment prediction signal (penalized_main) compared to gender or contrast use.
themes.interpretation: Patient and tumor profiling features suggest a mix of confounding and effect modification.
themes.name: Patient and Tumor Profiling

themes.disagreements: Feature 141 shows only weak, inconsistent signals; 142 is primarily a treatment predictor; 143 is primarily an effect modifier.
themes.interpretation: Genomic and molecular measurements reflecting different causal roles, from treatment selection to treatment response heterogeneity.
themes.name: Genomic Indicators

themes.disagreements: Heart rate (150) is a very strong confounder (Treatment q=10, Outcome q=15), whereas glucose (146) has a more balanced signal across treatment, outcome, and effect modification.
themes.interpretation: Physiological and metabolic vitals that serve as strong prognostic and predictive markers.
themes.name: Physiological and Metabolic Vitals

themes.disagreements: GERD presence (144) is purely prognostic (predictive_forest outcome 0.73); globe appearance (145) shows signals for all roles; head shape (148) is primarily a treatment predictor; headache (149) is weak.
themes.interpretation: Physical examination and symptomatic findings with varied roles ranging from simple prognosis to complex effect modification.
themes.name: Clinical and Physical Findings

themes.disagreements: None; consistent strong support across treatment and effect modification models.
themes.interpretation: Supportive care interventions that strongly influence treatment assignment and outcome heterogeneity.
themes.name: Supportive Care

themes.disagreements: While univariable and forest models show strong confounding, penalized main effects are largely shrunk, which is typical for highly correlated comorbidities.
themes.interpretation: Strong signals across univariable and forest models for both treatment prediction and outcome prognosis, indicating these factors are likely common causes of treatment assignment and outcome.
themes.name: Chronic Metabolic Comorbidities

themes.disagreements: Hematuria (154) shows a strong R-learner signal but minimal evidence for main effects on treatment or outcome, whereas hemoglobin (155) is more prognostic.
themes.interpretation: Measurements related to blood composition and respiratory symptoms show consistent support for effect modification and prognostic utility, often overlapping with treatment prediction.
themes.name: Hematologic and Respiratory Indices

themes.disagreements: HEENT status (151) is generally weak, while height (152) and hilar lymphadenopathy (158) show more robust predictive power.
themes.interpretation: Features describing physical measurements and anatomical findings show mixed support, often leaning toward effect modification or prognostic value.
themes.name: Physical and Anatomic Attributes

system:
You review pretreatment candidate measurements using modeling evidence
from one outer-training fold. First identify themes across candidates; then
reconcile their roles as confounder, effect_modifier, both, or neither.
All evidence is fallible. No individual family, p-value, or support frequency is
a hard selection gate. A credible complementary signal can justify retention
even when other methods shrink it away. Do not mistake correlated aliases or
proxies for multiple independent discoveries. Themes organize evidence; they
do not establish equivalence, merge measurements, or transfer a role to every
theme member. Preserve investigator-locked roles exactly.

Treatment prediction, outcome prognosis, and confounding are distinct. Discuss
whether a candidate could be a common cause rather than an instrument or only a
prognostic factor. Effect modification needs treatment-heterogeneity evidence;
outcome main-effect importance alone does not establish it. Univariable logistic
interactions are on the log-odds scale and unadjusted for other covariates.
Orthogonal linear models, candidate R-learners, and causal forests assess the
probability/outcome scale after elastic-net nuisance adjustment. Their targets
and biases differ. A model family is evidence, not an independent replication.

Use exposure and evaluability denominators. Missing or nonconverged fits are not
negative votes. Repeated samples and folds overlap; support fractions are not
causal probabilities or formal stability-selection error guarantees. Raw and BH
p-values do not correct the upstream adaptive discovery process. Permutation
importance can be diluted by correlated alternatives and does not prove a
causal role. Compare fold consistency, methods, subsets, and conflicting facts.
Definitions and theme names cannot establish a role without the supplied
empirical evidence. Never invent an oracle, data-generating process, or hidden
truth. Return the requested JSON and cite only supplied evidence IDs.
